question:
A 28-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after a previous visit showed an elevated serum calcium level. He has a history of bipolar disorder. His mother had a parathyroidectomy in her 30s. The patient does not drink alcohol or smoke. Current medications include lithium and a daily multivitamin. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Serum
Sodium 146 mEq/L
Potassium 3.7 mEq/L
Calcium 11.2 mg/dL
Magnesium 2.3 mEq/L
PTH 610 pg/mL
Albumin 4.2 g/dL
24-hour urine
Calcium 23 mg
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s findings?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Elevated serum calcium level" -> "High PTH level" -> "Possible primary hyperparathyroidism" -> 70% CHAIN: "Bipolar disorder history" -> "Lithium use" -> "Possible lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism" -> 60% CHAIN: "Family history of parathyroidectomy" -> "Possible genetic predisposition to parathyroid disorders" -> 50% CHAIN: "Normal physical examination" -> "Unlikely to be due to malignancy" -> 80% CHAIN: "Excess calcium intake" -> "Less likely due to low 24-hour urine calcium" -> 70% CHAIN: "Abnormal calcium sensing receptors" -> "Possible but less common cause" -> 60% CHAIN: "Excess vitamin D intake" -> "Less likely due to high PTH level" -> 70% CHAIN: "Lithium toxicity" -> "Possible cause due to lithium's effect on parathyroid glands" -> 60% CHAIN: "Parathyroid adenoma" -> "Most likely cause given high PTH and calcium levels" -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most likely cause of the patient's findings is a parathyroid adenoma, given the high PTH and calcium levels. The patient's history of bipolar disorder and lithium use may contribute to lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism. Excess calcium intake is less likely due to low 24-hour urine calcium. Abnormal calcium sensing receptors and excess vitamin D intake are also less likely causes. The evidence path linking lithium to physiological aspects of the parathyroid gland supports the potential role of lithium in this context.
analysis: The patient presents with elevated calcium and PTH levels, suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Given the history of bipolar disorder and lithium use, lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism is a likely cause. Excess calcium intake is less likely due to low 24-hour urine calcium. Abnormal calcium sensing receptors and excess vitamin D intake are also less probable. The evidence linking lithium to hyperparathyroidism supports this conclusion.
